title: Wimbledon recap Day 5: Novak Djokovic and Jannik Sinner stay on collision course
author: Ava Wallace
content:
Follow The Athletic’s Wimbledon coverage

Welcome to the Wimbledon briefing, where The Athletic will explain the stories behind the stories on each day of the tournament.

On Day 5, the two alpha dogs in the men’s draw rolled on, a great champion broke new ground and it was time to look deeper into a surprise result.

A Wimbledon semifinal between defending champion and top seed Jannik Sinner and seven-time winner Novak Djokovic feels increasingly inevitable.

The main obstacles in front of them are not their next couple of opponents, but extraneous factors. In Sinner’s case, it’s the potential for warmer weather next week, which has been his kryptonite previously. In Djokovic’s case, it’s the fact that at 39, he needs to keep his matches relatively quick lest he run out of energy in the latter rounds.

Italy’s Sinner, 24, hasn’t been at his devastating best yet and was uncharacteristically up and down again against Jenson Brooksby on Friday. Sinner was broken twice in the third set, but returned well enough to get the match done, 6-4, 6-3, 6-4.

“A small step forward,” Sinner said of his performance in a post-match news conference.

Serbia’s Djokovic had a trickier time of it against France’s No. 25 seed Arthur Rinderknech, but won 7-5, 6-4, 1-6, 7-6(4) in just over three hours. The length of the match was significant given the need for energy preservation that Djokovic spoke about last year and at the French Open in May. The relative speed of the match for a four-setter was, in part, down to a rapid third set that took barely 20 minutes, and which Djokovic seemed pretty uninterested in after Rinderknech had raced to a 4-0 lead.

He was impressively able to lock back in for the fourth set, which he took on a tiebreak. Djokovic also said in his post-match news conference that he feels fresher than he did in Paris, and that the grass takes less out of him than the clay.

Not that they especially need it, but the draws for their next-round matches have been kind to Sinner and Djokovic. Both are up against qualifiers, a rare occurrence in the fourth round of a Slam. Sinner takes on Japan’s world No. 151 Shintaro Mochizuki, while Djokovic is up against Roman Safiullin, the Russian 2023 Wimbledon quarterfinalist now ranked No. 132 after a string of injuries.

Sinner would then have an unseeded opponent in the quarters — either Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz or Germany’s Jan-Lennard Struff. For Djokovic, it would be either Félix Auger-Aliassime, the Canadian No. 3 seed who has little grass-court pedigree, or Alejandro Davidovich Fokina, the No. 22 seed from Spain who won his first ATP Tour title on the grass at the Mallorca Championships last month.

— Charlie Eccleshare

A year ago, when Naomi Osaka lost in the third round of Wimbledon, she was seriously annoyed.

It didn’t matter that grass had troubled her throughout her career. Her section of the draw was wide open. She had an opportunity. She felt like she had lost something.

Maybe that was the beginning of Osaka’s evolution on grass. She made the fourth round of Wimbledon for the first time Saturday, beating Australia’s Daria Kasatkina 6-1, 6-3.

“Every time I was going to return serve, like 120 mph was coming, so I mean it makes it difficult,” Kasatkina said in a news conference. “You have a lot of pressure on yourself because if you will lose your serve, it’s basically you’re in a very tough situation.”

Opponents haven’t historically felt that sort of pressure against Osaka on grass. They do now. She said in her news conference that she has finally started getting used to the free-flowing nature of grass-court tennis. She’s using the surface to help her, not fighting it.

It’s working — almost as well as those walk-on outfits that have become the talk of the tournament.

She faces world No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka, who beat Latvia’s Jelena Ostapenko 6-4, 6-4, next. That should be a big moment on Centre Court for their fourth meeting of the year.

“I think the Centre Court here for some reason might be the scariest Centre Court to me,” Osaka said. “Going down those stairs, it’s the opening, like this huge dome. I feel more aware of it than any other Centre Court that I’ve ever played on.”

— Matt Futterman

At first glance, an elder qualifier beating a highly rated teenage seed seems like it would be a huge upset. In the case of Roman Safiullin’s defeat of No. 24 seed João Fonseca 6-3, 6-3, 6-3? Not so much.

Safiullin, 28, was world No. 36 as recently as 2024 and made the Wimbledon quarterfinals in 2023. He hit over 40 winners against Fonseca and made just 18 unforced errors, saving several break points as the 19-year-old Brazilian tried to find a way back into the contest.

“He was playing very aggressive, going for the shots, going for the net,” Fonseca said in a news conference after the match. “He was courageous in the important points. Most of the important points he went to the net, went for the ball, and I couldn’t get the opportunities.”

“Of course, sometimes was my fault, but it happens. … I mean, even on grass, which is faster, the serves are difficult to return. I don’t think it was all my fault.”

Before Safiullin turned pro, he won the Australian Open junior title and promptly suffered severe injuries to his shoulder and ankle that hindered his development. More recently, the Russian was out between last September and this February. There is little wonder why he was in tears on No. 2 Court after beating Fonseca to set up a fourth-round match against Djokovic.

“After U.S. Open, I had to stop to treat my injury,” Safiullin said in his on-court interview. “That time was super tough. Even half a year ago, I didn’t know if I’d be able to be back.”

Fitness comes and goes, but talent does not go away.

That doesn’t mean there were no upsets. Jan-Lennard Struff, the 36-year-old German who came through five sets in both his first- and second-round matches, stunned No. 8 seed Daniil Medvedev 7-6(4), 7-6(5), 7-5, despite Medvedev leading by a break of serve in each of the first two sets and by two breaks in the third. And Mochizuki, the qualifier from Japan, defeated Spanish No. 23 seed Rafael Jódar — one of Fonseca’s peers — 1-6, 7-6(5), 6-4, 6-4. Mochizuki will meet Sinner in the fourth round while Struff will face Hurkacz, who defeated No. 21 seed Tommy Paul of the U.S. 4-6, 7-6(5), 7-5, 6-2.

— James Hansen

While it isn’t rare in tennis to play against a compatriot, most players agree that sharing nationality with an opponent adds meaning to a match.

There’s often a level of intimacy which, if the players are close in age, can stem from having grown up together within a national federation. If they’re not, odds are they’ve gotten to know each other through playing team competitions such as the Davis Cup or the Billie Jean King Cup.

For Wimbledon No. 4 seed Jessica Pegula, U.S. tennis is so well represented at major tournaments these days that facing another American is motivating because it activates her competitive side. She wants to come out as the top American — and beyond that, she wants to represent U.S. tennis well and give the fans a good match.

“I’m always motivated to beat the other Americans in a way that’s different,” she said in a news conference after beating Spain’s Jéssica Bouzas Maneiro 6-1, 6-3 in the third round. “Not like I don’t like them or anything like that. … There’s so many of us that there is always like this push-and-pull kind of battle in a fun way.”

Pegula should be feeling extra fiery for her next couple of matches. She faces American Iva Jović in the fourth round, a fast-rising 18-year-old who was born in California to a Serbian father and a Croatian mother.

Jović is a natural mover on grass and is self-assured, with an aggressive game and preternatural poise that makes it easy for her to move on when she makes mistakes on court — her go-to move when her serve abandoned her Thursday in a tight 6-3, 3-6, 6-4 third-round win against No. 18 seed Ekaterina Alexandrova was to shoot a glare and a spectacular eye-roll at her coaching box, then promptly reset.

Jović plans to rely on that same short-term memory in Sunday’s match against Pegula, to whom she’s lost twice this year.

“I think it’s just kind of how it is,” Jović said in a news conference. “Early in your career, you’re probably going to lose your first couple meetings against players who are already at the top, until you find your groove. And I think I have been proving in general that I’m getting closer, that I’m climbing, and playing better and better tennis. I hope that that can show.

“I don’t take too much weight to the fact that she’s beaten me twice, because I’m at a stage where I feel like I’m constantly changing as a player.”

Pegula’s changing, too, growing more comfortable on Wimbledon’s grass after a first-round exit last year and a second-round exit in 2024. She’s well aware of the dangers of facing a fellow American — a younger, hungry American playing freely with little to lose, at that.

“I know she’s going to come after me hard,” Pegula said. “I’ll use that as motivation and try to be ready for as much as I can.”

— Ava Wallace

Novak Djokovic and Arthur Rinderknech ended their match with a superb point that left both men flat out on the grass:

⚽ Why one rising American tennis star credits soccer for her success on grass during the World Cup.

🎓 For this player’s senior year, it was all about graduation and Grand Slams.

💗 Why Wimbledon holds a special place in one doubles star’s heart.

🎾 Women’s singles: Alexandra Eala (29) vs. Iga Świątek (3)

8:30 a.m. ET on ESPN, ESPN Unlimited

Eala announced herself to the tennis world by beating Świątek at last year’s Miami Open. Świątek got a measure of revenge at the Madrid Open, played on clay, so by the end of this Centre Court meeting, they will have played on all three surfaces. Eala, the 20-year-old from the Philippines, can stay low to the grass and fizz the ball over the net to rush 25-year-old Świątek’s preparation, but the 2025 champion from Poland met a similar challenge in her previous round against 2021 finalist Karolína Plíšková and won easily. Eala’s movement, especially parallel to the baseline, will be key to her chances.

🎾 Women’s singles: Amanda Anisimova (6) vs. Madison Keys (26)

10:30 a.m. ET on ESPN, ESPN Unlimited

As with Aryna Sabalenka and Jelena Ostapenko’s third-round match, pray for the tennis balls. Anisimova, last year’s finalist, found her serve just at the right time to scrape past Sofia Kenin in the previous round, with her timing on her forehand having been all over the place. But the 24-year-old American much prefers playing the likes of Keys, 31, in matches that can descend into first-strike blitzes. Don’t look for a ton of long rallies in this one.

🎾 Men’s singles: Grigor Dimitrov (WC) vs. Matteo Berrettini

12:30 p.m. ET on ESPN, ESPN Unlimited

A real opportunity for two proper grass-court players to make an impact in the bottom half of a wide-open men’s draw. Berrettini, 30, and Dimitrov, 35, can both pelt serves into the corners of the boxes and cut the ball low to the court with their slice backhands. They are both also recovering from periods of injury and rehab — Bulgaria’s Dimitrov for the first real time in his career; Italy’s Berrettini the latest of many. Berrettini has an edge on serve, but Dimitrov’s topspin backhand is far more penetrating and may prove the difference.

🎾 Men’s singles: Frances Tiafoe (17) vs. Alexander Bublik (10)

1 p.m. ET on ESPN, ESPN Unlimited

Two entertainers, who can light up a tennis court with aggressive, creative play. Two members of the top 20 who have struggled with motivation and never quite know whether or not they can, or will, or have the will to produce their best tennis. But all of a sudden they are in a land of opportunity at a Grand Slam. Who will seize the moment?

Tell us what you noticed on the fifth day…
